Opening — where we are, and what "optimising" means

⏱ 0:00–4:00
🖥 Slides 3–4

Topic 6 closes the course. In Topics 1 to 5 you built a monitoring setup for Atelier Nordik inc., the fictional 14-person design firm of Lab 1: you mapped the network, installed a monitoring server (MON-250), built a baseline, configured alerts, collected logs and traffic, detected anomalies, diagnosed one case (A-09) and reported it. Today we ask the question that every monitoring operator asks after the first month: is this setup as good as it can be, and how do we prove it?

Optimisation, in this course, has a precise meaning: a measured improvement of one property of the monitoring setup, verified by a test and recorded as a change. It is not "making things better" in general. The competency statement of the course (EZ01, element 5) lists the five properties we optimise, and they are the five sub-topics of today: the currency of the reference databases (6.1), the cost of monitoring for the network (6.2), the coverage of monitoring (6.3), the quality of the results (6.4), and the recommendation that documents the improvements (6.5).

🖥 Slide 5

All five sub-topics use the same four-step loop, shown in Figure 6.0-1: measure (a number, never an opinion), change one thing (one rule, one filter, one source at a time), verify (a back-test: replay the last weeks and confirm that the known incidents are still detected and that approved activity is no longer reported), and record (what, why, who, when, expiry date, review date). The loop is what distinguishes an optimisation from an undocumented change. An operator who changes a threshold without a back-test and without a record has not optimised anything; he has created a change that nobody can audit, which is precisely the kind of change that caused case A-09 in Class 16.

🖥 Slide 6

Everything today refers to the same network and the same cases: SRV-AD01 (192.168.10.5, criticality 5), OPNsense-FW (criticality 5), srv-web01 (192.168.20.10 in the DMZ (demilitarized zone), criticality 4), MON-250 (192.168.10.250, the monitoring and log server, criticality 4), the designer workstation WS-10-44, WS-10-31 and the twelve workstations of the pool (fourteen workstations in all, criticality 2). The alerts of the weekend of October 9-11 (A-01 to A-12), the baseline of WS-10-44 from Class 15, the Thursday evening traffic capture of Class 14 and case A-09 (failed antivirus definition updates after an unverified change) are the raw material of the five examples. Each example produces one file of the Lab 3 "Optimise" step: a new baseline version, a monitoring budget, a coverage matrix, a tuning record and a ranked recommendation list with its owner memo.

6.1 Updating the reference databases

⏱ 4:00-15:00
Learning outcome. Explain what a reference database is, list the five families used by a monitoring setup, update a baseline without contaminating it with an incident, and record the update as a change.
🖥 Slide 8

What a reference database is

A reference database is any stored description of what is known or normal, against which a detector compares an observation. The course outline uses the term for the baseline (the profile of normal activity built in Topic 3.4), but a working monitoring setup relies on five families of references, shown in Figure 6.1-1:

  1. the baseline: statistics of normal activity per host, per hour, per account (for WS-10-44: the mean and the standard deviation of outbound TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connection attempts for each hour of the day, computed over ten workdays);
  2. the asset inventory with its criticality scale (1 to 5), which tells the triage of Topic 5.2 how much an alert matters;
  3. the known-good lists: the allowlist (addresses, accounts and patterns that are approved), the maintenance calendar (approved activity with a start, an end, an asset and a scope) and the list of service accounts;
  4. the detection references: antivirus definitions, intrusion-detection rule sets (Suricata, Snort), reputation lists and threat-intelligence feeds - descriptions of what is known to be bad everywhere, not only here;
  5. the vulnerability references: the CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) feed of the vulnerability scanner and the software version inventory.

The first three families describe this network; they can only come from our own observation and our own change process. The last two describe the outside world; they come from a publisher and must be downloaded. The distinction matters for the update method: a local reference is updated by recomputing, an external reference by fetching and verifying.

🖥 Slide 9

Why references age

A reference is correct on the day it is built and becomes less correct every day after. Three processes make it age. Drift: normal activity changes - a new designer joins, a project moves working hours into the evening, a software update doubles the number of connections of an application. The baseline of September does not describe October. New threats: a detection reference that has not been refreshed cannot recognise a signature published after its last update; the Cyber Centre's guidance on updates (ITSAP.10.096) treats an outdated system as a vulnerability in itself, and an outdated detection reference is the same problem on the monitoring side. New assets: a device that is not in the inventory has no criticality, is in no coverage matrix and receives no monitoring - an attacker can use it, but no rule and no analyst watches it.

Because aging is continuous, every reference gets an age metric: the time since its last successful update. The age is a key performance indicator (KPI) with a target: definitions no older than 8 hours (two update cycles of 4 hours), the baseline no older than 35 days, the inventory updated the same day as any change, the calendar updated at the moment a change is approved. The KPI (Key Performance Indicator) turns "are we up to date?" into a number that a rule can watch.

🖥 Slide 10

Updating a baseline without poisoning it

Recomputing a baseline is a statistical operation with four rules. First, use a bounded window: the last four to six weeks of workdays, so that the profile follows the drift but does not react to one unusual day. The baseline keeps the sample count, the mean and the standard deviation per hour and per week; the weeks inside the window are pooled, and an old week is dropped by leaving it out of the pool, not by subtracting it. In the example the window has three weeks so far (September 21 to October 9), so nothing is dropped yet. Second, apply exclusions: hours that belong to a confirmed incident never enter the statistics. If the scan hours of Thursday October 8 were included, the mean of the 19:00 hour would move from 3 to about 6 and its standard deviation from 1.5 to about 12; the next scan at 19:00 would produce a z-score of 3.5 instead of 29, and the 14 connections of the 20:00 hour would score 3.2 - both at the edge of the threshold after one contaminated week, and below it after two. Teaching the baseline that an attack is normal is called baseline poisoning (also contamination), and it is the most common way a detector loses sensitivity without any rule being changed.

Third, approved activity that is different from the ordinary day goes into its own profile. The Patch-Wednesday hours (first Wednesday of the month, 14:00-16:00, from the maintenance calendar) produce 112 connections where the workday mean is 63; mixing them into the workday profile would widen the band for every Wednesday. We keep a separate "patch-day" profile, and we use it only when it has at least five samples (a course rule: minimum sample count); until then the calendar provides the context. Fourth, version the file (baseline_hourly_v2.csv next to v1) and write a change record: for each hour, the old statistics, the values added, the values excluded and the new statistics. A reference database is never edited in place.

The combination itself does not need the old samples. Call the old group n1 samples with mean m1 and standard deviation s1, and the new group k samples with mean m2 and standard deviation s2. The pooled mean is the sample-count-weighted average (n1 x m1 + k x m2) / (n1 + k). The pooled variance adds the two within-group variances, each weighted by its degrees of freedom (n1 - 1 and k - 1), and the two squared differences between each group mean and the pooled mean, each weighted by its sample count, and divides the sum by n1 + k - 1; the formula is written out in the script and in step 3 of the example. This is why the baseline file stores n, the mean and the standard deviation, and not the raw counts.

🖥 Slides 11–12

Updating detection references with verification

External references are fetched, and fetching is the step where errors occur most often. The update procedure of Figure 6.1-3 has six steps and each one leaves a trace: (1) source - the official publisher, over an authenticated channel, never a mirror found by a search engine; (2) verify the origin - compare the published hash or signature and the version number (the Legal Notice, section 14.2 and Annex C, asks for a VirusTotal check of any downloaded file); (3) test - in the lab first, with a snapshot; for a baseline, a back-test over the last week; (4) deploy - inside a maintenance-calendar window, with a rollback; (5) verify the effect - the KPI (Key Performance Indicator) moved as expected and the known incidents are still detected; (6) record - version, date, who, what changed, why.

Two consequences follow. A failed update is a monitoring-health event: by the hand rule of Class 15 it is never triaged below P2, because a reference that stops updating removes protection silently. And an update of a reference database is a change in the sense of the change process: it needs a ticket, a window in the calendar and a verification step - the three things that were missing from change CH-2026-090 in case A-09. The frequency differs by family (definitions every 4 hours automatically, rule sets daily, feeds hourly, the baseline monthly, the inventory and the calendar at every change), the procedure does not.

🖥 Slides 13–14

Example 6.1 - Refreshing the baseline of WS-10-44 (Lab 3 Optimise, deliverable 1)

Task
Update the hourly baseline of the designer workstation WS-10-44 with the observed week of October 6-9, excluding the confirmed scan hours of Thursday October 8 (19:00-21:00) and keeping the Patch-Wednesday hours in a separate profile; then back-test the observed week against the new baseline and write the change record.
Relation to 6.1
This is sub-topic 6.1 applied to the first family of reference databases: a rolling-window update, with exclusions and a maintenance profile, versioned and verified by a back-test. The same inputs were used in Class 15 (baseline_hourly.csv, observed_week.csv) and the same detector (z-score 3, minimum absolute difference 10), so the comparison before/after is fair.
Part of Lab 3
Lab 3, Part 3 'Optimise' - deliverable 1: baseline_hourly_v2.csv + baseline_change_record.csv (and baseline_backtest.csv as the verification). In your lab report, quote the three hours whose mean moved the most and explain each move.
Language
Python 3 (standard library only) — update_baseline.py
Inputs
data/baseline_hourly.csv - 24 rows: hour, mean, stdev, n (10 workdays, Sept 21 - Oct 4)
data/observed_week.csv - 96 rows: Tue Oct 6 00:00 to Fri Oct 9 23:00
data/exclusions.csv - the incident window (CASE-2026-015)
data/maintenance_calendar.csv - Patch Wednesday, backup windows, vendor sync, weekly scan
Outputs
outputs/baseline_hourly_v2.csv (24 hours, n = 13 or 14)
outputs/baseline_patchday.csv (2 hours, marked 'insufficient')
outputs/baseline_change_record.csv
outputs/baseline_excluded_hours.csv
outputs/baseline_backtest.csv (v1: 3 alerts, v2: 3 alerts; with calendar context: 2 alerts + 1 INFO)

The code (a comment before every line explains what it does and why) Python 3 (standard library only)

update_baseline.py⬇ Download
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# ============================================================================
# update_baseline.py  -  Example 6.1 (Topic 6.1, Updating the reference databases)
# Course 420-1C1-DW Preventative Monitoring - Cyber.SoHo Educational Hub
#
# TASK: refresh the hourly baseline of WS-10-44 (reference database "normal activity")
#       with the observed week Tue Oct 6 - Fri Oct 9, 2026, WITHOUT teaching it the
#       confirmed incident hours (Thu Oct 8 19:00-21:00) and WITHOUT mixing the
#       Patch-Wednesday maintenance hours into the ordinary workday profile.
#       The script writes baseline_hourly_v2.csv, baseline_patchday.csv, a change
#       record and a back-test of the observed week against the new baseline.
# LAB 3 (Part 3 "Optimise"): deliverable 1 = baseline_hourly_v2.csv + baseline_change_record.csv.
# Usage:  python3 update_baseline.py  (run from the folder that contains the data/ folder)
# Legal: educational material, isolated lab data only - see the Cyber.SoHo Legal Notice,
#        Terms of Use and Acceptable Use Policy (sections 6.7 and 7.2).
# ============================================================================

# Import the csv module, because every reference database of this course is a plain CSV file that any tool can read.
import csv
# Import math for the square root used when a variance is turned back into a standard deviation.
import math
# Import os so the script can build file paths that work on Windows, Linux and macOS.
import os
# Import datetime so that timestamps can be compared with the calendar and the exclusion windows.
from datetime import datetime

# The folder that holds the input files; "data" sits next to the folder of this script.
DATA = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)), "..", "data")
# The folder that receives the results, so that inputs are never overwritten (a reference database is versioned, never edited in place).
OUT = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)), "..", "outputs")
# The z-score threshold of the detector from Class 15, reused for the back-test so that the comparison is fair.
Z_THRESHOLD = 3.0
# The minimum absolute difference guard from Class 15: a deviation below 10 connections is never reported, whatever its z-score.
MIN_ABS_DIFF = 10
# The smallest number of samples an hour needs before its statistics are trusted as a baseline (a rule of this course, not a law of statistics).
MIN_SAMPLES = 5
# The time format used in every CSV file of the scenario (local time, Montreal, EDT).
FMT = "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M"


# A helper that reads a CSV file into a list of dictionaries, one per row, so that each column is reached by its name.
def read_csv(name):
    # Open the file with UTF-8 so that French accents in descriptions never break the script.
    with open(os.path.join(DATA, name), newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        # Return the rows as dictionaries; the header line gives the keys.
        return list(csv.DictReader(f))


# A helper that writes a list of dictionaries to a CSV file in the outputs folder.
def write_csv(name, rows, fields):
    # Create the outputs folder on the first run so that the script never fails on a fresh checkout.
    os.makedirs(OUT, exist_ok=True)
    # Open the destination file for writing; newline="" prevents blank lines on Windows.
    with open(os.path.join(OUT, name), "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        # Build a writer that knows the column order.
        w = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=fields)
        # Write the header line first so that spreadsheets and other scripts understand the file.
        w.writeheader()
        # Write every row in order.
        w.writerows(rows)


# A helper that tells whether a timestamp falls inside any window of a list (used for exclusions and for the calendar).
def inside(ts, windows, asset):
    # Walk through every window of the list.
    for win in windows:
        # Keep only the windows that concern this asset (or a pool that contains it, or "*" meaning every asset).
        if win["asset"] not in (asset, "WS-pool", "*"):
            # Skip the windows of other assets.
            continue
        # Convert the start of the window to a datetime for comparison.
        start = datetime.strptime(win["start"], FMT)
        # Convert the end of the window to a datetime for comparison.
        end = datetime.strptime(win["end"], FMT)
        # A timestamp is inside when it is at or after the start and strictly before the end.
        if start <= ts < end:
            # Return the matching window so that the caller can record WHY the hour was treated differently.
            return win
    # No window matched: the hour is an ordinary hour.
    return None


# A helper that merges the old statistics (n1, mean1, stdev1) with k new samples, using only summary numbers.
def pooled(n1, m1, s1, samples):
    # The number of new samples added to this hour.
    k = len(samples)
    # When there is nothing to add, the old statistics are returned unchanged.
    if k == 0:
        # Return a tuple in the same order as the input so that callers do not need a special case.
        return n1, m1, s1
    # The mean of the new samples.
    m2 = sum(samples) / k
    # The sample variance of the new samples (k-1 in the denominator); a single sample has no variance of its own.
    v2 = sum((x - m2) ** 2 for x in samples) / (k - 1) if k > 1 else 0.0
    # The total number of samples after the update.
    n = n1 + k
    # The pooled mean is the sample-count-weighted average of the two means.
    m = (n1 * m1 + k * m2) / n
    # The pooled variance combines the two within-group variances and the two shifts of the group means (exact formula).
    v = ((n1 - 1) * s1 ** 2 + (k - 1) * v2 + n1 * (m1 - m) ** 2 + k * (m2 - m) ** 2) / (n - 1)
    # Return the new count, the new mean and the new standard deviation (square root of the variance).
    return n, m, math.sqrt(v)


# The main procedure, so that the steps run in a fixed, teachable order.
def main():
    # STEP 1 - load the current reference database (baseline v1) into a dictionary keyed by hour of day.
    base = {int(r["hour"]): {"n": int(r["n"]), "mean": float(r["mean"]), "stdev": float(r["stdev"])} for r in read_csv("baseline_hourly.csv")}
    # STEP 1 - load the observed week (96 hourly counts).
    observed = read_csv("observed_week.csv")
    # STEP 1 - load the exclusion windows (confirmed incidents must never become "normal").
    exclusions = read_csv("exclusions.csv")
    # STEP 1 - load the maintenance calendar (approved, scheduled activity that is normal but different).
    calendar = read_csv("maintenance_calendar.csv")
    # Print a short header so that the operator sees which inputs were used.
    print(f"[1] loaded baseline v1 ({len(base)} hours), {len(observed)} observed hours, {len(exclusions)} exclusion window(s), {len(calendar)} calendar entries")

    # STEP 2 - sort every observed hour into one of three buckets: ordinary, excluded (incident) or maintenance.
    ordinary, excluded, maintenance = {}, [], {}
    # Walk through the observed hours in chronological order.
    for r in observed:
        # Parse the timestamp of the row.
        ts = datetime.strptime(r["timestamp"], FMT)
        # Read the count as an integer.
        count = int(r["count"])
        # First check the exclusion windows, because an incident takes precedence over everything else.
        win = inside(ts, exclusions, "WS-10-44")
        # An hour inside an incident window is recorded as excluded and never reaches the statistics.
        if win:
            # Keep the reason, so that the change record can be audited later.
            excluded.append({"timestamp": r["timestamp"], "count": count, "reason": win["reason"], "case": win["case"]})
            # Move on to the next hour.
            continue
        # Then check the maintenance calendar: a scheduled activity is normal, but it belongs to its own profile.
        win = inside(ts, calendar, "WS-10-44")
        # An hour inside a maintenance window is stored in the "patch day" profile, keyed by hour of day.
        if win:
            # Append the count to the list of that hour in the maintenance profile.
            maintenance.setdefault(ts.hour, []).append(count)
            # Move on to the next hour.
            continue
        # Everything else is an ordinary workday hour and feeds the main baseline.
        ordinary.setdefault(ts.hour, []).append(count)
    # Report the sorting so that the class can check the three buckets.
    print(f"[2] sorted: {sum(len(v) for v in ordinary.values())} ordinary hours, {len(excluded)} excluded hours, {sum(len(v) for v in maintenance.values())} maintenance hours")

    # STEP 3 - combine the old statistics with the ordinary samples, hour by hour, and keep a change record.
    v2, changes = {}, []
    # Walk through the 24 hours of the day in order.
    for h in range(24):
        # Fetch the old statistics of this hour.
        old = base[h]
        # Fetch the new ordinary samples of this hour (an empty list when all of them were excluded).
        samples = ordinary.get(h, [])
        # Compute the pooled count, mean and standard deviation.
        n, m, s = pooled(old["n"], old["mean"], old["stdev"], samples)
        # Store the result as baseline v2.
        v2[h] = {"hour": h, "mean": round(m, 2), "stdev": round(s, 2), "n": n, "profile": "workday"}
        # Record what changed and why, because a reference database update is a change like any other.
        changes.append({"hour": h, "old_n": old["n"], "old_mean": old["mean"], "old_stdev": old["stdev"], "added": len(samples),
                        "added_values": " ".join(str(x) for x in samples), "excluded": sum(1 for e in excluded if datetime.strptime(e["timestamp"], FMT).hour == h),
                        "new_n": n, "new_mean": round(m, 2), "new_stdev": round(s, 2), "delta_mean": round(m - old["mean"], 2)})
    # Report the largest movements so that the operator can judge whether the update looks plausible.
    biggest = sorted(changes, key=lambda c: abs(c["delta_mean"]), reverse=True)[:3]
    # Print the three hours whose mean moved the most.
    print("[3] pooled 24 hours; largest mean changes:", ", ".join(f"{c['hour']:02d}:00 {c['old_mean']}->{c['new_mean']}" for c in biggest))

    # STEP 4 - build the maintenance ("patch day") profile from the maintenance samples, flagged until it has enough samples.
    patch = []
    # Walk through the hours that received maintenance samples.
    for h, samples in sorted(maintenance.items()):
        # A profile with fewer than MIN_SAMPLES values is kept for information but marked as not usable for detection yet.
        status = "usable" if len(samples) >= MIN_SAMPLES else f"insufficient ({len(samples)} of {MIN_SAMPLES}) - keep using the calendar as context"
        # Store the hour, the mean of the maintenance samples, the number of samples and the status.
        patch.append({"hour": h, "mean": round(sum(samples) / len(samples), 2), "n": len(samples), "status": status, "profile": "patch-wednesday"})
    # Report the second profile.
    print(f"[4] patch-day profile: {len(patch)} hour(s) -> " + "; ".join(f"{p['hour']:02d}:00 mean {p['mean']} ({p['status']})" for p in patch))

    # STEP 5 - back-test: re-run the Class 15 detector over the observed week with baseline v2 and compare with v1.
    backtest = []
    # Walk again through the observed week.
    for r in observed:
        # Parse the timestamp and the count.
        ts, count = datetime.strptime(r["timestamp"], FMT), int(r["count"])
        # Fetch the v1 and v2 statistics of this hour of day.
        o, nw = base[ts.hour], v2[ts.hour]
        # Compute the z-score against v1 (guard against a zero standard deviation).
        z1 = (count - o["mean"]) / o["stdev"] if o["stdev"] else 0.0
        # Compute the z-score against v2.
        z2 = (count - nw["mean"]) / nw["stdev"] if nw["stdev"] else 0.0
        # Apply the detector rule for v1: |z| at or above the threshold AND an absolute difference of at least MIN_ABS_DIFF.
        f1 = abs(z1) >= Z_THRESHOLD and abs(count - o["mean"]) >= MIN_ABS_DIFF
        # Apply the same rule for v2.
        f2 = abs(z2) >= Z_THRESHOLD and abs(count - nw["mean"]) >= MIN_ABS_DIFF
        # The context of the hour (maintenance window or excluded incident) is recorded separately: the detector itself ignores it in both runs.
        ctx = "maintenance" if inside(ts, calendar, "WS-10-44") else ("excluded-incident" if inside(ts, exclusions, "WS-10-44") else "")
        # A third column shows what the 6.4 context enrichment would do with the v2 flag: a flagged maintenance hour becomes INFO, not ALERT.
        with_cal = ("INFO" if ctx == "maintenance" else "ALERT") if f2 else ""
        # Keep one row per observed hour with both verdicts and the calendar-aware verdict.
        backtest.append({"timestamp": r["timestamp"], "count": count, "z_v1": round(z1, 2), "flag_v1": "ALERT" if f1 else "", "z_v2": round(z2, 2), "flag_v2": "ALERT" if f2 else "", "flag_v2_with_calendar": with_cal, "context": ctx})
    # Count the alerts under each version with the identical detector: a correct refresh changes no verdict.
    a1 = sum(1 for b in backtest if b["flag_v1"] == "ALERT")
    # The same count for v2.
    a2 = sum(1 for b in backtest if b["flag_v2"] == "ALERT")
    # The hours whose verdict changed between v1 and v2 (expected: none).
    changed = [b["timestamp"] for b in backtest if (b["flag_v1"] == "ALERT") != (b["flag_v2"] == "ALERT")]
    # Print the comparison, then the effect of the calendar context, which belongs to Topic 6.4 and is reported separately.
    print(f"[5] back-test over 96 hours with the same detector: v1 = {a1} alerts, v2 = {a2} alerts, verdicts changed: {len(changed)} {changed if changed else '(known incidents still detected, nothing new flagged)'}; with the calendar context of 6.4: {sum(1 for b in backtest if b['flag_v2_with_calendar'] == 'ALERT')} alerts + {sum(1 for b in backtest if b['flag_v2_with_calendar'] == 'INFO')} INFO")

    # STEP 6 - write the versioned reference database, the second profile, the change record and the back-test.
    write_csv("baseline_hourly_v2.csv", list(v2.values()), ["hour", "mean", "stdev", "n", "profile"])
    # Write the patch-day profile.
    write_csv("baseline_patchday.csv", patch, ["hour", "mean", "n", "status", "profile"])
    # Write the change record (the audit trail of this update).
    write_csv("baseline_change_record.csv", changes, list(changes[0].keys()))
    # Write the excluded hours with their reasons, so that nobody wonders later why they are missing.
    write_csv("baseline_excluded_hours.csv", excluded, ["timestamp", "count", "reason", "case"])
    # Write the back-test.
    write_csv("baseline_backtest.csv", backtest, list(backtest[0].keys()))
    # Print the final line that the operator pastes into the change ticket.
    print("[6] written: baseline_hourly_v2.csv, baseline_patchday.csv, baseline_change_record.csv, baseline_excluded_hours.csv, baseline_backtest.csv  (version v2, source window 2026-09-21 .. 2026-10-09, incidents excluded: CASE-2026-015)")


# Run the main procedure only when the file is executed directly (not when it is imported by a test).
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Start.
    main()

Run it here, step by step (the simulator executes the same logic on the same data)

Step-by-step explanation

  1. Step 1 - load. The script reads the four input files. The baseline becomes a dictionary keyed by hour of day (0-23); the observed week is a list of 96 rows; the exclusions and the calendar are lists of windows with a start, an end and an asset.
  2. Step 2 - sort the observed hours into three buckets. For each of the 96 hours: if the timestamp is inside an exclusion window for WS-10-44 it goes to excluded (2 hours: Oct 8 19:00 and 20:00); otherwise, if it is inside a maintenance window that applies to the workstation pool, it goes to maintenance (2 hours: Oct 7 14:00 and 15:00); everything else is ordinary (92 hours). The order of the tests matters: an incident takes precedence over the calendar.
  3. Step 3 - pool, hour by hour. For each hour of the day the old statistics (n = 10) are combined with the ordinary samples of that hour (4 values, or 3 when one went to the exclusion list or to the maintenance profile). The pooled mean is (n1 x m1 + k x m2) / (n1 + k). The pooled variance is [(n1 - 1) s1^2 + (k - 1) s2^2 + n1 (m1 - m)^2 + k (m2 - m)^2] / (n1 + k - 1). The change record stores old and new values and the samples added. In October the three largest moves were 10:00 (66.0 to 69.1), 17:00 (30.0 to 32.6) and 11:00 (64.0 to 61.6) - all small, as expected for a stable workstation.
  4. Step 4 - build the patch-day profile. The two maintenance hours form a second profile with n = 1 each. The script marks them 'insufficient (1 of 5)': the profile is kept for information, and the calendar remains the context used by the detector until five Patch Wednesdays have been observed.
  5. Step 5 - back-test. The Class 15 detector (same thresholds, no calendar) is run twice over the same 96 hours, once with v1 and once with v2. Result: both versions flag the same three hours - the Patch-Wednesday hour (z 3.27 under v1, 3.67 under v2) and the two scan hours (z 33.9 and 9.3 under v2). This is the result expected from a correct refresh: the known incidents are still detected and no verdict changed. The approved activity is still flagged by the baseline alone; it becomes INFO only when the detector consults the maintenance calendar - the context enrichment of 6.4, reported by the script in a separate column (2 alerts + 1 INFO). Two limits to state in the lab report: the back-test replays the same week that fed v2 (in-sample), so the real test is the following week; and the reduction of alerts comes from the calendar, not from the new statistics.
  6. Step 6 - write and record. Five files are written. Nothing is overwritten: v1 stays on disk next to v2, and the last line printed by the script is the sentence that goes into the change ticket (version, source window, exclusions).

6.2 Reducing the impact of monitoring on network performance

⏱ 15:00-25:00
Learning outcome. Name the four cost components of monitoring, choose a collection strategy that keeps every detection the rules depend on, and measure the cost before and after a change.
🖥 Slide 17

Monitoring has a cost, and the cost has four components

Monitoring is itself a workload on the network it observes. The performance impact of monitoring is the sum of four measurable components, listed in Figure 6.2-1: bandwidth (the mirrored copy of the traffic, log forwarding, flow export, management polling); host resources (the processor time and memory used by agents, by a verbose audit policy or by a local capture); collector storage (every byte received by MON-250 is written, indexed and kept for the retention period); and sensor capacity (a sensor that receives more frames than it can process drops some of them, and a dropped frame is an event that never existed for the detector). A fifth cost is not technical but real: every gigabyte stored is a gigabyte that an analyst must be able to search during an investigation.

The lesson of Topic 1.5 applies in reverse here: a performance problem caused by monitoring is not a security problem, but it will be treated as one by the users who complain, and it is the fastest way to have the monitoring switched off. The operator's duty is therefore to know the cost in numbers before and after any change of collection.

🖥 Slide 18

Passive collection: SPAN (Switched Port Analyzer), TAP (Test Access Point), inline

The placement of the sensor determines the load on the production network. A SPAN (Switched Port Analyzer) session, also called port mirroring, asks the switch to copy the frames of one or more ports to the sensor port. The copy costs the production links nothing, but the mirror port has the speed of one port, and the two directions of the mirrored link add up on it: an uplink running at 600 Mbit/s in each direction produces a 1.2 Gbit/s copy, and above 1 Gbit/s the switch silently discards part of the copy. At Atelier Nordik the SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) poller measures the uplink at 38 Mbit/s on average and 420 Mbit/s at its peak, both directions added together, so the copy fits the 1 Gbit/s mirror port with a margin. A network TAP (Test Access Point) is a passive device inserted in the cable; it never drops and never loads the switch, but it needs a second sensor interface and a short interruption of the link to install (450 CAD (Canadian dollars) in the proposal of Example 6.5). An inline sensor (an intrusion prevention system in the path of the traffic) adds latency to every packet and becomes a point of failure: if it stops, the network stops or the protection stops, depending on its fail-open or fail-closed setting. In a 14-person firm with one operator, passive collection is the default and inline devices are reserved for the perimeter.

🖥 Slide 19

Reducing the volume: filters, flows and sampling - and what each one loses

Three techniques reduce the bytes that reach the collector, and each one removes a specific kind of information. A capture filter (written in the Berkeley Packet Filter syntax, BPF, understood by tcpdump and Wireshark) discards known-good bulk conversations at the sensor, before they are written: the SMB (Server Message Block) backup copies to SRV-AD01 and the HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) downloads from the vendor mirror represent 88 % of the bytes of the Thursday sample and carry no detection value. The loss is explicit: those two conversations become invisible, and the coverage matrix of 6.3 must say so. Flow records (NetFlow and the standard IPFIX (IP Flow Information Export); sFlow is a sampled variant with the limits of sampling described below) replace the packets of a conversation by one record per 5-tuple (source address, destination address, protocol, source port, destination port) with counters: bytes, packets, flags, start and end time. A flow exporter on the firewall sees every conversation that crosses the firewall - LAN (Local Area Network) to DMZ (demilitarized zone), LAN (Local Area Network) to WAN (Wide Area Network), VPN (Virtual Private Network) to LAN (Local Area Network) - at 1 to 8 % of the packet volume (8 % in our small-packet sample, 1 to 3 % on a typical office link); traffic that stays inside one segment, such as the SMB (Server Message Block) backup from WS-10-44 to SRV-AD01, never reaches it and must be covered by the LAN (Local Area Network) mirror or by the authentication logs. The loss is the payload: who talked to whom, when and how much, never what was said. Sampling keeps one frame in N. It is the cheapest and the most dangerous reduction for security: at 1:10 the 16 frames of a port scan lasting under 20 seconds keep on average 1.6 frames, far below the 10-port rule, and the six SYN (synchronize flag of TCP) frames to port 4444 (sent 10 seconds apart) survive with a probability of only about 47 % (1 - 0.9 to the power 6); in the sample of Example 6.2 none of the 22 frames survived (Figure 6.2-3). Sampling is acceptable for capacity planning, not for detection rules that count events.

🖥 Slide 20

Reducing the load at the source

The second group of techniques acts on the monitored hosts. Log level and filtering at the source: keep every security event (Windows 4624, 4625, 4688, Defender 2000 and 2001; Linux authentication records) and drop debug and verbose application records before they leave the host; the measure is events per second per source. Polling interval: a management station that polls a device by SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) every 10 seconds generates thirty times the management traffic and device processor time of one poll every 5 minutes; utilisation counters are polled every 5 minutes, and urgent states (a link going down) are reported by traps, which the device sends on its own. Scheduling: heavy jobs - the weekly vulnerability scan, a full capture, the re-indexing of the log store - run outside business hours and are written in the maintenance calendar, otherwise they become alerts (the Sunday 04:00 scan produced four false alarms in Example 6.4). Buffering and compression on the forwarders smooth bursts and survive short outages of the collector. Rotation and tiered retention (90 days searchable, one year compressed) keep the disk of MON-250 under its alert threshold (A-01 was the disk at 86 %).

🖥 Slide 21

Measure before and after; the one rule that ranks above cost

A reduction is a change, so it follows the loop: measure the KPI (Key Performance Indicator) before (mirror-port utilisation in percent, sensor drop counter, gigabytes written per day, events per second per source, processor use of the agent on a workstation), change one thing, measure after, record. The rule that ranks above every saving is: never remove the data that a detection rule depends on. Each reduction must be traced to the rules it affects - a capture filter that drops port 445 also drops the evidence of the next SMB-based lateral movement inside the LAN (Local Area Network), unless the authentication logs (and, for traffic that crosses the firewall, the flow records) still cover it. This is why 6.3 (coverage) is decided before 6.2 (cost): the cheapest strategy that keeps every needed detection is the right one, not the cheapest strategy.

Collecting less also has a legal side. Monitoring data is treated as personal information in this course (Legal Notice, section 7.2), and Québec's private-sector privacy law (the Act respecting the protection of personal information in the private sector, as amended by Law 25) asks organisations to collect only what is necessary and to keep it only as long as necessary. A monitoring budget that stores 410 GB of full packets per day "in case" is both a performance problem and a data-minimisation problem.

Example 6.2 - The monitoring budget of the LAN (Local Area Network) mirror (Lab 3 Optimise, deliverable 2)

Task
From the 5-minute sample capture of WS-10-44 taken on Thursday October 8 (packets.csv, 68 frames) and the SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) utilisation of the mirrored LAN (Local Area Network) uplink (38 Mbit/s average, 420 Mbit/s peak, both directions added together), compute the gigabytes per day that MON-250 would receive under four collection strategies - full capture, filtered capture, flow records, 1:10 sampling - the retention each allows on a 500 GB budget, and whether the two detections of Example 4.2 (16-port scan, 6 unanswered SYN (synchronize flag of TCP) to port 4444) survive each strategy.
Relation to 6.2
This is sub-topic 6.2 measured instead of discussed: the four cost components become one table, and the rule 'never remove the data a detection depends on' becomes two yes/no columns. The script uses only bash and awk, the tools available on any Linux sensor, so that the same measurement can be repeated on MON-250.
Part of Lab 3
Lab 3, Part 3 'Optimise' - deliverable 2: monitoring_budget.csv. In your proposal, recommend one strategy per segment (LAN (Local Area Network) mirror, DMZ (demilitarized zone), VPN (Virtual Private Network)) and justify it with the two detection columns.
Language
Bash + awk (Linux shell) — estimate_capture_load.sh
Inputs
data/packets.csv - 68 frames, tshark field export of Class 14 (frame.time, ip.src, ip.dst, ip.proto, tcp.srcport, tcp.dstport, tcp.flags, frame.len)
data/snmp_utilisation.csv - average and peak Mbit/s per segment, from the SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) poller
Outputs
outputs/monitoring_budget.csv - one row per strategy: sample bytes, share of full, GB/day, retention days at 500 GB, scan detected, SYN-4444 detected, side effect

The code (a comment before every line explains what it does and why) Bash + awk (Linux shell)

estimate_capture_load.sh⬇ Download
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# ============================================================================
# estimate_capture_load.sh  -  Example 6.2 (Topic 6.2, Reducing the impact of monitoring on network performance)
# Course 420-1C1-DW Preventative Monitoring - Cyber.SoHo Educational Hub
#
# TASK: measure, from the 5-minute sample capture of WS-10-44 (packets.csv, Class 14 format) and the
#       SNMP utilisation of the mirrored LAN link (snmp_utilisation.csv), how many bytes per day the
#       monitoring server MON-250 would have to receive and store under four collection strategies:
#       (A) full packet capture, (B) filtered capture (known-good bulk flows removed at the sensor),
#       (C) flow records only (NetFlow/IPFIX style, one record per 5-tuple), (D) 1-in-10 packet sampling.
#       For each strategy the script also checks whether the two detections of Example 4.2
#       (16-port scan of srv-web01, 6 unanswered SYN to 198.51.100.200:4444) would still be visible.
# LAB 3 (Part 3 "Optimise"): deliverable 2 = monitoring_budget.csv (the "monitoring budget" of the proposal).
# Usage: bash estimate_capture_load.sh        (needs bash 4+, awk, sort - present on any Linux)
# Legal: educational material, isolated lab data only - Cyber.SoHo Legal Notice sections 6.7 and 7.2.
# ============================================================================

# Stop at the first error, treat unset variables as errors and make a failing command inside a pipe fail the pipe: safer scripts.
set -euo pipefail

# Locate the folder of this script so that the data and outputs folders are found whatever the current directory is.
HERE="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
# The input folder.
DATA="$HERE/../data"
# The output folder (created if missing; inputs are never modified).
OUT="$HERE/../outputs"
# Create the output folder.
mkdir -p "$OUT"

# Size of the per-packet record header that libpcap adds in a capture file (16 bytes), needed for an honest "full capture" size.
PCAP_RECORD_HEADER=16
# Size of one flow record in a NetFlow v5 export (48 bytes); IPFIX records are similar in size.
FLOW_RECORD_BYTES=48
# Sampling ratio of strategy D: one frame in ten is kept (the sampler keeps every 10th frame).
SAMPLE_EVERY=10
# Storage budget of MON-250 for packet data (gigabytes) - the figure from the Lab 1 monitoring plan.
STORAGE_GB=500
# Average utilisation (Mbit/s) of the mirrored LAN link, read from the SNMP file (first data line, column 2).
AVG_MBPS=$(awk -F, 'NR==2 {print $2}' "$DATA/snmp_utilisation.csv")
# Peak utilisation (Mbit/s) of the same link, used to warn about a saturated SPAN port.
PEAK_MBPS=$(awk -F, 'NR==2 {print $3}' "$DATA/snmp_utilisation.csv")

# STEP 1 - announce the inputs so that the operator sees what the estimate is based on.
echo "[1] sample: $(($(wc -l < "$DATA/packets.csv") - 1)) frames from packets.csv; mirrored link average ${AVG_MBPS} Mbit/s, peak ${PEAK_MBPS} Mbit/s (SNMP)"

# STEP 2 - strategy A: add up every frame length plus the capture-file record header (full packet capture).
FULL=$(awk -F, -v h="$PCAP_RECORD_HEADER" 'NR>1 {b += $9 + h} END {print b}' "$DATA/packets.csv")
# Report the number of bytes a full capture of the sample would occupy.
echo "[2] A full capture of the sample      : ${FULL} bytes"

# STEP 3 - strategy B: drop the two known-good bulk conversations at the sensor (SMB backup to SRV-AD01:445 and HTTPS to the vendor mirror 203.0.113.80).
# (In production this is a capture filter, for example: not (host 192.168.10.5 and port 445) and not (host 203.0.113.80 and port 443).)
FILTERED=$(awk -F, -v h="$PCAP_RECORD_HEADER" 'NR>1 && !(($3=="192.168.10.5"||$4=="192.168.10.5") && ($6==445||$7==445)) && !(($3=="203.0.113.80"||$4=="203.0.113.80") && ($6==443||$7==443)) {b += $9 + h} END {print b}' "$DATA/packets.csv")
# Report the filtered size.
echo "[3] B filtered capture of the sample  : ${FILTERED} bytes (SMB backup and vendor HTTPS removed at the sensor)"

# STEP 4 - strategy C: aggregate the frames into flows (same 5-tuple: source, destination, protocol, source port, destination port) and count one 48-byte record per flow.
FLOWS=$(awk -F, 'NR>1 {key=$3"|"$4"|"$5"|"$6"|"$7; f[key]=1} END {n=0; for (k in f) n++; print n}' "$DATA/packets.csv")
# Multiply the number of flows by the size of one flow record.
FLOWBYTES=$((FLOWS * FLOW_RECORD_BYTES))
# Report the flow-record size.
echo "[4] C flow records of the sample      : ${FLOWS} flows x ${FLOW_RECORD_BYTES} bytes = ${FLOWBYTES} bytes"

# STEP 5 - strategy D: keep every 10th frame (deterministic 1:10 sampling) and add up the kept bytes.
SAMPLED=$(awk -F, -v h="$PCAP_RECORD_HEADER" -v s="$SAMPLE_EVERY" 'NR>1 && (NR-1)%s==0 {b += $9 + h} END {print b}' "$DATA/packets.csv")
# Report the sampled size.
echo "[5] D 1:${SAMPLE_EVERY} sampled capture of the sample: ${SAMPLED} bytes"

# STEP 6 - check which detections of Example 4.2 survive each strategy.
# Count the distinct destination ports of the scan (WS-10-44 -> srv-web01 192.168.20.10, SYN only) in the full sample.
SCAN_PORTS=$(awk -F, 'NR>1 && $3=="192.168.10.44" && $4=="192.168.20.10" && $8=="SYN" {p[$7]=1} END {n=0; for (k in p) n++; print n}' "$DATA/packets.csv")
# Count the unanswered SYN frames to 198.51.100.200:4444 in the full sample.
SYN4444=$(awk -F, 'NR>1 && $4=="198.51.100.200" && $7==4444 && $8=="SYN" {n++} END {print n+0}' "$DATA/packets.csv")
# Count the same two things in the sampled capture (every 10th frame only).
SCAN_PORTS_S=$(awk -F, -v s="$SAMPLE_EVERY" 'NR>1 && (NR-1)%s==0 && $3=="192.168.10.44" && $4=="192.168.20.10" && $8=="SYN" {p[$7]=1} END {n=0; for (k in p) n++; print n}' "$DATA/packets.csv")
# Count the SYN-to-4444 frames that survive the sampling.
SYN4444_S=$(awk -F, -v s="$SAMPLE_EVERY" 'NR>1 && (NR-1)%s==0 && $4=="198.51.100.200" && $7==4444 && $8=="SYN" {n++} END {print n+0}' "$DATA/packets.csv")
# Count the scan flows (distinct destination ports to srv-web01) that a flow exporter would report.
SCAN_FLOWS=$(awk -F, 'NR>1 && $3=="192.168.10.44" && $4=="192.168.20.10" {p[$7]=1} END {n=0; for (k in p) n++; print n}' "$DATA/packets.csv")
# The detection rules of Class 14: a scan needs 10 or more distinct ports in 60 s; the SYN rule needs at least one SYN without any reply.
echo "[6] detections: scan ports seen - full/filtered ${SCAN_PORTS}, flows ${SCAN_FLOWS}, sampled ${SCAN_PORTS_S} (rule: >=10) ; SYN to 4444 - full/filtered ${SYN4444}, flows ${SYN4444} one-packet flows with no reply flow, sampled ${SYN4444_S}"

# STEP 7 - scale the sample to one day of the mirrored link: bytes/day = average Mbit/s / 8 x 86 400 s; each strategy keeps the same share of bytes as in the sample.
awk -v avg="$AVG_MBPS" -v peak="$PEAK_MBPS" -v full="$FULL" -v filt="$FILTERED" -v flow="$FLOWBYTES" -v samp="$SAMPLED" \
    -v sp="$SCAN_PORTS" -v sf="$SCAN_FLOWS" -v ss="$SCAN_PORTS_S" -v y="$SYN4444" -v ys="$SYN4444_S" -v budget="$STORAGE_GB" 'BEGIN {
      # Bytes carried by the mirrored link in one day at the average utilisation (1 Mbit = 1 000 000 bits).
      day = avg * 1000000 / 8 * 86400;
      # Print the header of the monitoring budget file.
      print "strategy,sample_bytes,share_of_full,GB_per_day,retention_days_at_" budget "GB,scan_detected,syn4444_detected,side_effect";
      # One line per strategy: the share of the sample it keeps is applied to the daily volume of the link.
      printf "A full capture,%d,%.3f,%.1f,%.1f,%s,%s,%s\n", full, 1.0, day/1e9, budget/(day/1e9), (sp>=10?"yes":"no"), (y>=1?"yes":"no"), "SPAN port saturates above 1 Gbit/s (peak " peak " Mbit/s is fine); disk fills in days";
      printf "B filtered capture,%d,%.3f,%.1f,%.1f,%s,%s,%s\n", filt, filt/full, day/1e9*filt/full, budget/(day/1e9*filt/full), (sp>=10?"yes":"no"), (y>=1?"yes":"no"), "the two filtered conversations are invisible afterwards: document them in the coverage matrix";
      printf "C flow records,%d,%.3f,%.2f,%.0f,%s,%s,%s\n", flow, flow/full, day/1e9*flow/full, budget/(day/1e9*flow/full), (sf>=10?"yes":"no"), (y>=1?"yes (flows with 0 reply packets)":"no"), "no payload: cannot see what was sent, only who talked to whom, when and how much";
      printf "D sampled 1:10,%d,%.3f,%.1f,%.1f,%s,%s,%s\n", samp, samp/full, day/1e9*samp/full, budget/(day/1e9*samp/full), (ss>=10?"yes":"no"), (ys>=1?"yes":"no"), "short events are missed most of the time: the 16-frame scan cannot reach the 10-port rule, the six SYN frames survive about half of the time";
    }' > "$OUT/monitoring_budget.csv"
# Show the resulting table on the screen.
echo "[7] monitoring budget (bytes per day on the mirrored link at ${AVG_MBPS} Mbit/s average):"
# Pretty-print the first five columns of the CSV as aligned columns (awk only, so that the script needs no extra package).
awk -F, '{printf "    %-20s %12s %10s %10s %10s %6s %s\n", $1, $2, $3, $4, $5, $6, $7}' "$OUT/monitoring_budget.csv"

# STEP 8 - final advice line: the strategy must keep every detection the rules depend on (6.3) before it saves bytes (6.2).
echo "[8] written: $OUT/monitoring_budget.csv - choose the cheapest strategy that still shows every detection you depend on (B for the LAN mirror, C for the DMZ and VPN segments)"

Run it here, step by step (the simulator executes the same logic on the same data)

Step-by-step explanation

  1. Step 1 - inputs. The script counts the frames of the sample (68) and reads the average (38 Mbit/s) and peak (420 Mbit/s) utilisation of the mirrored link from the SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) file with awk. These two numbers are the scale factor: the sample tells us the share each strategy keeps, the SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) numbers tell us the volume of the link.
  2. Step 2 - strategy A, full capture. awk adds the length of every frame plus the 16-byte record header that a capture file stores per frame: 27 665 bytes for the sample.
  3. Step 3 - strategy B, filtered capture. The same sum, excluding the two known-good bulk conversations (SMB (Server Message Block) to SRV-AD01 port 445 and HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) with the vendor mirror 203.0.113.80): 3 224 bytes, 11.7 % of the full capture. In production the same condition is a BPF (Berkeley Packet Filter) capture filter on the sensor.
  4. Step 4 - strategy C, flow records. awk groups the frames by 5-tuple (46 flows) and counts 48 bytes per flow record (the size of a NetFlow version 5 record): 2 208 bytes, 8 % of the sample. On a real office link the share is lower (1-3 %) because most bytes travel in a few long flows.
  5. Step 5 - strategy D, 1:10 sampling. awk keeps every tenth frame: 469 bytes, 1.7 %. Cheapest by far.
  6. Step 6 - detections. The script counts the distinct destination ports of the scan (16, rule needs 10) and the unanswered SYN (synchronize flag of TCP) frames to 198.51.100.200:4444 (6, rule needs 1) in the full sample, in the flow records and in the sampled frames. Full, filtered and flow strategies keep both detections; sampling keeps neither (0 scan ports, 0 SYN (synchronize flag of TCP) frames survive: Figure 6.2-3).
  7. Step 7 - scale to one day. Bytes per day of the link (both directions, as measured by the poller) = 38 x 1 000 000 / 8 x 86 400 = 410 GB. Each strategy keeps its share: A 410 GB/day (1.2 days of retention on 500 GB), B 47.8 GB/day (10.5 days), C 32.75 GB/day (15 days), D 7 GB/day (72 days, but no detections). The side-effect column records what each strategy loses.
  8. Step 8 - decision. The cheapest strategy that keeps every detection: B (filtered capture) for the LAN (Local Area Network) mirror, where packet detail is needed for the signatures, and C (flow export from the firewall) for the DMZ (demilitarized zone) and VPN (Virtual Private Network) segments that are not mirrored at all. D is rejected for detection, and A is rejected for cost. The decision goes into the Lab 3 proposal with this table as evidence.

6.3 Improving monitoring coverage

⏱ 25:00-36:00
Learning outcome. Define coverage, build a coverage matrix from assets, data sources and detection needs, compute a weighted coverage score, rank the gaps and add source-health monitoring.
🖥 Slide 26

What coverage is

Monitoring coverage is the share of what we need to observe that we actually observe. It has three dimensions: the assets (every device of the inventory, weighted by criticality), the data sources (authentication logs, process creation logs, antivirus health, firewall decisions, VPN (Virtual Private Network) sessions, flow records, packet mirrors, web server logs, DNS (Domain Name System) queries, time synchronisation) and the detection needs (the questions the rules and the analysts must be able to answer). The instrument that shows coverage is the coverage matrix: assets in rows, sources in columns, each cell marked collected, available but not collected, missing, or not applicable (Figure 6.3-1). A cell that is required and not collected is a gap; a gap that prevents a question from being answered is a blind spot.

Coverage is not the same as volume. In October the LAN (Local Area Network) mirror delivers 410 GB of packets per day and the coverage score is still 58.8 %, because the volume comes from one segment while the gaps are on the firewall, the VPN (Virtual Private Network), the DMZ (demilitarized zone) and the workstations' process logs. Lab 3 made the blind spots concrete: the five open questions of Part C - which VPN (Virtual Private Network) account held 10.8.0.9, whether any logon on srv-web01 succeeded after the guessing, which process on WS-10-44 opened the connections, whether the firewall blocked the SYNs (synchronize flags of TCP) to port 4444, why srv-web01 went silent - cannot be answered with the data collected today, and neither can two further needs (the DMZ (demilitarized zone) side of the scan, one time line for correlation): seven of the eight needs of the coverage matrix are blocked.

🖥 Slide 27

Seven ways coverage is lost

  1. Source not collected: the device produces the data but nobody forwards it (OPNsense keeps its filter log locally for seven days; the nginx access log stays on srv-web01).
  2. Event type not enabled: the audit policy does not record process creation (Windows event 4688) and no Sysmon is installed, so no host can say which program opened a connection.
  3. Segment not observed: only the LAN (Local Area Network) uplink is mirrored; the DMZ (demilitarized zone) side of a conversation and the VPN (Virtual Private Network) pool are invisible to the sensor.
  4. Silent source: srv-web01 stopped sending at 11:20 on Saturday (A-12) and nobody was told, because no rule watches the sources themselves.
  5. Clock drift: WS-10-31 is 2.4 seconds off (A-07); events of two hosts cannot be placed on one time line and correlation fails.
  6. Retention too short: a question asked on Tuesday about Thursday evening needs the records to still exist; the firewall's seven local days are not enough for a 90-day investigation window.
  7. Encrypted or summarised traffic: the packet mirror sees HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) to the vendor but not its content; only flows, DNS (Domain Name System) and the TLS (Transport Layer Security) handshake metadata remain informative.

The joint guidance Best practices for event logging and threat detection (led by the Australian Cyber Security Centre and co-signed by the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, the American agencies and other partners, August 2024) lists the same conditions from the organisation's side: an approved logging policy, centralised collection and correlation, secure storage with integrity, and a detection strategy for the threats that matter.

🖥 Slide 28

Needs, techniques and sources

A detection need is written as a question with the sources that answer it. The questions come from three places: the open items of the investigations (Lab 3), the rules we run, and the attack techniques we have decided to see. For the last group this course uses the MITRE ATT&CK knowledge base (version 19 since April 2026): each technique has known data sources, so a technique chosen as a detection goal names the sources required. Figure 6.3-3 maps the eight needs of October: a brute-force attempt (T1110) needs authentication logs and a live source; the identity behind a VPN (Virtual Private Network) address (T1133 External Remote Services) needs the VPN (Virtual Private Network) session log; the program behind a scan (T1046 Network Service Discovery) needs process creation events; a connection on an unusual port (T1571 Non-Standard Port) needs the firewall decision; an attacker who stops the tools (T1685 Disable or Modify Tools, under the tactic TA0112 Defense Impairment) needs antivirus health and source-health events. Table T6-3-1 gives the full list of sources with the techniques each one helps to see and how it is collected at Atelier Nordik.

🖥 Slide 29

The coverage method and the score

The method has seven steps (Figure 6.3-2): list the needs; list the assets with criticality; record the status of each source per asset; build the matrix; compute the score; rank the gaps; close them, cheapest first on equal weight. The coverage score is weighted by criticality: the sum of (criticality x collected cells) over the sum of (criticality x required cells), with a partial source counting one half. The weighting makes the score reflect the importance of each asset - a missing source on the domain controller (criticality 5) costs five times a missing source on a workstation. The gap weight for ranking is criticality x the number of needs the gap blocks (at least 1), and ties go to the cheapest closure. The required sources per asset type are a reference database of their own (required_sources.csv) and are reviewed with the inventory.

🖥 Slide 30

Monitoring the monitoring: source health

The largest single improvement of coverage is usually not a new source but a rule about the existing ones. A source-health rule (a heartbeat) alerts when a source that normally produces events has produced none for a defined interval - 30 minutes for servers and the firewall in the proposal - and the alert is P2 by the hand rule, because silence is indistinguishable from an attacker who disabled logging. The rule needs two reference inputs: the expected rate of each source (a small baseline) and the maintenance calendar (a planned reboot is not silence). It closes need N5 and it would have found A-12 at 11:50 on Saturday instead of during triage on Sunday.

Example 6.3 - The coverage matrix of Atelier Nordik (Lab 3 Optimise, deliverable 3)

Task
Build the coverage matrix (7 assets x 13 sources) from the asset inventory, the required sources per asset type and the status of each source recorded during Labs 2 and 3; compute the criticality-weighted coverage score; evaluate the eight detection needs; rank the 14 gaps and attach one closure action with an effort estimate to each.
Relation to 6.3
This is sub-topic 6.3 as a procedure: the matrix, the score, the needs evaluation and the ranked gaps are the four outputs the lesson defined. The ranked gaps are the input of the recommendation list of Example 6.5.
Part of Lab 3
Lab 3, Part 3 'Optimise' - deliverable 3: coverage_matrix.csv + coverage_gaps_ranked.csv. In your report, state the score before, the score you expect after your top three closures, and which open questions of Part C become answerable.
Language
Python 3 (standard library only) — coverage_matrix.py
Inputs
data/assets.csv - asset, address, segment, type, criticality, owner
data/required_sources.csv - the sources an asset type must provide
data/sources.csv - status of every (asset, source) pair: collected / available_not_collected / not_enabled / absent, with a note
data/needs.csv - eight questions with the required asset:source pairs and the ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge) technique
Outputs
outputs/coverage_matrix.csv
outputs/coverage_needs.csv (1 answerable, 7 blocked)
outputs/coverage_gaps_ranked.csv (14 gaps)
outputs/coverage_summary.csv (score 58.8 %)

The code (a comment before every line explains what it does and why) Python 3 (standard library only)

coverage_matrix.py⬇ Download
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# ============================================================================
# coverage_matrix.py  -  Example 6.3 (Topic 6.3, Improving monitoring coverage)
# Course 420-1C1-DW Preventative Monitoring - Cyber.SoHo Educational Hub
#
# TASK: build the coverage matrix of the Atelier Nordik network (assets x data sources), compute a
#       criticality-weighted coverage score, find out which detection needs of Lab 3 are blocked by
#       missing sources, rank the gaps, and propose one closure action per gap.
# LAB 3 (Part 3 "Optimise"): deliverable 3 = coverage_matrix.csv + coverage_gaps_ranked.csv.
# Usage: python3 coverage_matrix.py
# Legal: educational material, isolated lab data only - Cyber.SoHo Legal Notice sections 6.7 and 7.2.
# ============================================================================

# csv reads and writes the plain-text tables used by the whole course.
import csv
# os builds file paths that work on every operating system.
import os

# The folder that holds the inputs (assets, sources, required sources, needs).
DATA = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)), "..", "data")
# The folder that receives the results.
OUT = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)), "..", "outputs")
# The order of the data sources in the matrix (columns), from authentication to time synchronisation.
SOURCE_ORDER = ["auth_log", "process_log", "av_health", "firewall_log", "vpn_log", "flow_export", "web_access_log",
                "syslog_forwarding", "packet_mirror_LAN", "packet_mirror_DMZ", "source_health", "disk_health", "ntp_sync"]
# One closure action per kind of source, used to turn a gap into a recommendation (input of Example 6.5).
CLOSURE = {
    "process_log": ("enable Audit Process Creation (event 4688) by group policy or deploy Sysmon", 3),
    "vpn_log": ("forward the OpenVPN status/log of OPNsense to MON-250 (remote syslog) to map account <-> 10.8.0.x", 2),
    "firewall_log": ("send the OPNsense filter log to MON-250 (remote syslog)", 2),
    "flow_export": ("enable NetFlow/IPFIX export on OPNsense towards an nfdump collector on MON-250", 2),
    "source_health": ("add a heartbeat rule: no event from a source for 30 min -> P2 alert", 1),
    "packet_mirror_DMZ": ("add a second SPAN session or a network TAP on the DMZ segment", 3),
    "web_access_log": ("forward the nginx access log with rsyslog", 1),
    "syslog_forwarding": ("configure the remote syslog target on the device", 1),
    "ntp_sync": ("point w32time/chrony to SRV-AD01 and alert on drift above 1 s", 1),
    "disk_health": ("lower the disk alert threshold and add a rotation policy", 1),
    "auth_log": ("enable and forward the authentication log", 1),
    "av_health": ("forward the Defender operational log (events 2000/2001)", 1),
    "packet_mirror_LAN": ("configure the SPAN session on the LAN switch", 2),
}


# Read a CSV file from the data folder into a list of dictionaries.
def read_csv(name):
    # UTF-8 keeps accents intact; newline="" is the csv-module convention.
    with open(os.path.join(DATA, name), newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        # Each row becomes a dictionary keyed by the header line.
        return list(csv.DictReader(f))


# Write a list of dictionaries to a CSV file in the outputs folder.
def write_csv(name, rows, fields):
    # Make sure the outputs folder exists.
    os.makedirs(OUT, exist_ok=True)
    # Open for writing.
    with open(os.path.join(OUT, name), "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        # A writer that respects the column order.
        w = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=fields)
        # Header first.
        w.writeheader()
        # Then the rows.
        w.writerows(rows)


# The main procedure runs the method of the lesson in six numbered steps.
def main():
    # STEP 1 - load the asset list with criticality (from Lab 1 / Class 15).
    assets = read_csv("assets.csv")
    # STEP 1 - load the required sources per asset type (what "complete coverage" means for each kind of device).
    required = {r["type"]: r["required_sources"].split(";") for r in read_csv("required_sources.csv")}
    # STEP 1 - load the current status of every (asset, source) pair, as found during Labs 2 and 3.
    status = {(r["asset"], r["source"]): r for r in read_csv("sources.csv")}
    # STEP 1 - load the detection needs (the open questions of Lab 3 and the lessons of Class 16).
    needs = read_csv("needs.csv")
    # Report the inputs.
    print(f"[1] {len(assets)} assets, {len(status)} (asset, source) pairs, {len(needs)} detection needs")

    # STEP 2 - build the matrix: one row per asset, one column per source, each cell = collected / partial / missing / n-a.
    matrix = []
    # Walk through the assets.
    for a in assets:
        # Start the row with the asset name and its criticality.
        row = {"asset": a["asset"], "criticality": a["criticality"]}
        # Walk through the sources in column order.
        for s in SOURCE_ORDER:
            # A source that this asset type does not need is marked "n-a" (not applicable).
            if s not in required[a["type"]]:
                # Not applicable cells never count in the score.
                row[s] = "n-a"
                # Next source.
                continue
            # Fetch the recorded status of this pair; an unrecorded pair is treated as absent (unknown = not collected).
            st = status.get((a["asset"], s), {"status": "absent"})["status"]
            # Translate the status into the three matrix values.
            row[s] = "collected" if st == "collected" else ("partial" if st == "available_not_collected" else "missing")
        # Add the row to the matrix.
        matrix.append(row)
    # Report the matrix size.
    print(f"[2] matrix built: {len(matrix)} rows x {len(SOURCE_ORDER)} source columns")

    # STEP 3 - score: criticality-weighted share of required cells that are collected (partial counts half).
    weight_total, weight_ok = 0, 0.0
    # Walk through the rows.
    for row in matrix:
        # Criticality of this asset (1 to 5).
        c = int(row["criticality"])
        # Walk through the cells.
        for s in SOURCE_ORDER:
            # Skip cells that do not apply.
            if row[s] == "n-a":
                # Next cell.
                continue
            # Every applicable cell adds its criticality to the denominator.
            weight_total += c
            # A collected cell adds its full weight, a partial cell half, a missing cell nothing.
            weight_ok += c if row[s] == "collected" else (c / 2 if row[s] == "partial" else 0)
    # The coverage score as a percentage.
    score = 100.0 * weight_ok / weight_total
    # Report the score.
    print(f"[3] weighted coverage score = {weight_ok:.1f} / {weight_total} = {score:.1f} %")

    # STEP 4 - evaluate every detection need: which required (asset:source) pairs are not collected?
    need_rows, blocked_by = [], {}
    # Walk through the needs.
    for n in needs:
        # The required pairs of this need, written "asset:source" and separated by semicolons.
        pairs = n["required"].split(";")
        # Collect the pairs that are not collected.
        missing = [p for p in pairs if status.get(tuple(p.split(":")), {"status": "absent"})["status"] != "collected"]
        # A need is answerable only when nothing is missing.
        verdict = "answerable" if not missing else "blocked"
        # Keep one row per need for the output.
        need_rows.append({"need_id": n["need_id"], "question": n["question"], "attack_technique": n["attack_technique"], "verdict": verdict, "missing": ";".join(missing), "reference": n["reference"]})
        # Count, for every missing pair, how many needs it blocks (used to rank the gaps).
        for p in missing:
            # Add this need to the list of needs blocked by the pair.
            blocked_by.setdefault(p, []).append(n["need_id"])
    # Report the verdicts.
    print(f"[4] needs: {sum(1 for r in need_rows if r['verdict']=='answerable')} answerable, {sum(1 for r in need_rows if r['verdict']=='blocked')} blocked")

    # STEP 5 - rank the gaps: weight = criticality of the asset x number of needs blocked, cheapest closure first on ties.
    crit = {a["asset"]: int(a["criticality"]) for a in assets}
    gaps = []
    # Walk through every applicable cell that is not collected.
    for row in matrix:
        # Walk through the sources.
        for s in SOURCE_ORDER:
            # Only partial and missing cells are gaps.
            if row[s] in ("partial", "missing"):
                # The pair name as used in needs.csv.
                pair = f"{row['asset']}:{s}"
                # The needs blocked by this pair (possibly none: a gap can exist without a current question).
                nb = blocked_by.get(pair, [])
                # The closure action and its effort (1 = minutes, 5 = days) from the table above.
                action, effort = CLOSURE.get(s, ("define a collection method", 3))
                # The ranking weight.
                weight = crit[row["asset"]] * max(1, len(nb))
                # Store the gap.
                gaps.append({"gap": pair, "status": row[s], "criticality": crit[row["asset"]], "needs_blocked": ";".join(nb) or "(none yet)", "weight": weight, "closure_action": action, "effort_1_to_5": effort, "note": status.get((row["asset"], s), {"note": ""})["note"]})
    # Sort by weight (descending), then by effort (ascending).
    gaps.sort(key=lambda g: (-g["weight"], g["effort_1_to_5"]))
    # Report the top three gaps.
    print("[5] top gaps: " + "; ".join(f"{g['gap']} (weight {g['weight']}, effort {g['effort_1_to_5']})" for g in gaps[:3]))

    # STEP 6 - write the matrix, the needs evaluation, the ranked gaps and a one-line summary.
    write_csv("coverage_matrix.csv", matrix, ["asset", "criticality"] + SOURCE_ORDER)
    # The needs evaluation.
    write_csv("coverage_needs.csv", need_rows, list(need_rows[0].keys()))
    # The ranked gaps.
    write_csv("coverage_gaps_ranked.csv", gaps, list(gaps[0].keys()))
    # The summary (one row) that the recommendation memo quotes.
    write_csv("coverage_summary.csv", [{"coverage_score_pct": round(score, 1), "gaps": len(gaps), "needs_blocked": sum(1 for r in need_rows if r["verdict"] == "blocked"), "needs_total": len(need_rows)}], ["coverage_score_pct", "gaps", "needs_blocked", "needs_total"])
    # Final line.
    print(f"[6] written: coverage_matrix.csv, coverage_needs.csv, coverage_gaps_ranked.csv, coverage_summary.csv  ({len(gaps)} gaps, score {score:.1f} %)")


# Run only when executed directly.
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Start.
    main()

Run it here, step by step (the simulator executes the same logic on the same data)

Step-by-step explanation

  1. Step 1 - load. Seven assets, 33 recorded (asset, source) pairs, eight needs. The required sources per asset type come from a small reference file so that 'complete coverage' is defined once, not per analyst.
  2. Step 2 - matrix. For each asset and each of the 13 sources: 'n-a' when the asset type does not require the source; otherwise the recorded status translated into collected, partial (available but not collected) or missing. An unrecorded pair is treated as missing: unknown is not collected.
  3. Step 3 - score. Each applicable cell adds the asset's criticality to the denominator and, when collected, to the numerator (half when partial): 70 / 119 = 58.8 %. The weight explains why the firewall row (criticality 5, four gaps) costs more than all workstation gaps together.
  4. Step 4 - needs. Each need lists its required pairs; the need is answerable only when every pair is collected. Result: N6 (failed definition updates) is answerable; N1 to N5, N7 and N8 are blocked, each by the pairs listed in the 'missing' column.
  5. Step 5 - rank the gaps. Weight = criticality x number of needs blocked (minimum 1); ties go to the lowest effort. The top three: srv-web01 source_health (weight 8, effort 1 - it blocks N2 and N5), SRV-AD01 source_health (5, effort 1), OPNsense syslog forwarding (5, effort 1). The closure action and the effort come from a table of standard actions (one per kind of source), so that two operators would propose the same action.
  6. Step 6 - write. The matrix, the needs evaluation, the ranked gaps and a one-row summary. The summary row is what the owner memo of Example 6.5 quotes ('coverage 59 %, target above 85 %').

6.4 Improving the quality and accuracy of results (fewer false alarms)

⏱ 36:00-48:00
Learning outcome. Measure the quality of a rule with precision and recall, explain why false alarms occur, apply the seven tuning methods with a back-test, and document every change with scope, owner and expiry.
🖥 Slide 35

Quality is measured with four outcomes and two ratios

Every rule produces one of four outcomes for each situation (Figure 6.4-2): a true positive (TP, a real event, an alert), a false positive (FP, no event, an alert - a false alarm), a false negative (FN, a real event, no alert - a miss) and a true negative (TN, nothing happened, no alert). Two ratios summarise them. Precision = TP (true positive) / (TP (true positive) + FP (false positive)) is the share of alerts that were correct; it is the ratio the analyst experiences directly, because it says how many of the alerts opened were worth opening. Recall (also sensitivity or detection rate) = TP (true positive) / (TP (true positive) + FN (false negative)) is the share of real events that were detected; it is what the organisation discovers after an incident. Tuning means raising precision without lowering recall: fewer false alarms and no new misses. Class 15 introduced a third category that belongs to the TP (true positive) column: the benign true positive, a correct alert about approved activity (the designer typing an old password eleven times). It is closed with a reason code, and the rule is left alone, because it did its job.

The numbers of the four weeks from September 14 to October 11: 51 alerts, 7 true, 2 benign, 42 false, 1 slow attack missed. Precision 0.18, recall 0.86. An analyst who opens nearly 13 alerts a week, of which fewer than two concern a real event, stops reading them - the condition is called alert fatigue and it is the mechanism by which a true alert is closed without being read.

🖥 Slide 36

Why false alarms occur

False alarms have identifiable causes, and the cause chooses the remedy. (1) A stale reference: a service account with a password changed by mistake generated 12 failed logons every night for four weeks - 28 of the 42 false alarms come from one cause, and the remedy is to fix the password (process), not the rule. (2) A rule without context: the baseline rule fired on Patch Wednesday because it did not consult the calendar. (3) A measure that does not represent the failure: the definition-age rule fired on laptops that were switched off (no events at all) and waited 36 hours on the real failure, because the age of the last success is not the same thing as a failed attempt. (4) Approved activity that looks like an attack: the authorised weekly scan from MON-250 and the vendor's contracted support session are indistinguishable from an attacker by their shape; only their source, target, time window and the contract make them legitimate. (5) A threshold on the wrong time scale: 10 failures in 10 minutes caught two fast attacks and missed a slow one at 8 failures per 10 minutes for an hour. The miss is a recall problem, and it was found only because the ground truth of the four weeks had been established during the investigations.

🖥 Slide 37

Seven tuning methods

Table T6-4-1 describes the methods; in order of preference: (1) threshold adjustment, always with a second slower condition rather than a higher single threshold (10 in 10 minutes or 30 in 60 minutes); (2) a scoped exception for one known, approved source of alerts; (3) context enrichment: the rule consults the calendar, the allowlist or the asset criticality before deciding; (4) correlation: two independent signals are required before an alert (failures and a success; a scan and an outbound connection from the same host); (5) aggregation: one alert per source per window with the count inside, instead of one alert per event; (6) a rule logic change: replace the measured quantity when it does not represent the failure (age of last success replaced by two consecutive failed attempts); (7) closure with a reason code for benign true positives - no change to the rule. Every method is tested the same way: a replay of the last four weeks of alerts and of the known events through the proposed rule set, which must show false alarms down, misses not up, and the detection delay measured.

🖥 Slide 38

The shape of a scoped exception, and the record

Exceptions are the tuning method with the highest risk of creating blind spots. A scoped exception names all of: the asset, the account or the source address, the time window, the activity (the logon type, the target), the owner, the reason and an expiry date (Figure 6.4-3). "Ignore nas-sync" would also ignore an attacker who steals the nas-sync credentials; "nas-sync on SRV-AD01, 01:00-01:10, logon type 4, until November 15" ignores exactly one failing job. An exception without an expiry date is a permanent blind spot that persists after its reason has disappeared. The tuning change record has one line per change: rule, what changed, before, after, scope, reason, owner, expiry, review date. A rule that is disabled is recorded in the same place - tuning by deletion leaves no trace and is forbidden by the loop. The monthly review reads the record, removes expired exceptions and lists the ten noisiest rules with their false-alarm reasons; that list is the input of the next tuning cycle.

🖥 Slide 39

Detection delay against false alarms: the A-09 rule

The definition-update rule shows that quality has a time dimension. Version 1 compared the age of the last successful update with 24 hours, once a day at 09:30: it alerted 36 hours and 15 minutes after the first failure of case A-09 and it fired five times on laptops that were simply off. Version 2 counts consecutive failed attempts (Defender event 2001) on the same host and alerts at the second one: 4 hours after the first failure, 8 hours after the last success in the worst case, and never on a silent host - a host that sends nothing is a coverage question (6.3), not a failure. The mean time to detect (MTTD) falls from 36.25 hours to 4, the false alarms fall from 5 to 0, and recall stays at 1. The replay of Example 6.4 is what proves it; without the replay the change is an opinion.
